title: estimate $\sin 46°$ to 4 d.p. and bound the error
panels: $\sin 46°$ correct to four decimals, with a proof of that accuracy, not a calculator reading.
$46°=45°+1°$: $\sin 45°$ and $\cos 45°$ are exact, and $h=\pi/180$ is small.
keypoints: $h$ must be in radians.
The remainder keeps $\cos$ at an unknown $\xi$.
$|R_{2}|\le h^{3}/6$ is the whole accuracy proof.

title: $D^{n}(x^{2}e^{x})$ by Leibniz
panels: A closed formula in $n$ for the high derivatives of a product.
$x^{2}$ dies after two derivatives; $e^{x}$ never changes.
keypoints: Choose as $u$ the factor that eventually vanishes.
$\binom{n}{2}2=n(n-1)$: the 2 cancels.

title: find the Taylor series of $y=\arcsin x$ about $x=0$
keypoints: Start from the ODE, never from $\arcsin$ directly.
Coefficient equals $y^{(n)}(0)/n!$.

title: ratio test on the sine series
panels: Powers and factorials: the ratio cancels the factorial.
Absolutely convergent for every finite $x$; radius $R=\infty$.
keypoints: $(2r+3)!=(2r+3)(2r+2)(2r+1)!$ gives the denominator.
$x$ is frozen while $r\to\infty$.

title: Leibniz on $x^{2}e^{x}$: $D^{2}$ and $D^{10}$
panels: Two high derivatives from one formula.
keypoints: Same template as $x^{3}e^{x}$, fewer rows.

title: Leibniz on $x^{3}e^{x}$ to $n=5$
panels: Four candidate rows for $n\ge3$; for $n=1$ only two.
keypoints: $\binom{n}{3}6$ loses its 6 to the denominator.

title: the arcsin recurrence in one poster
panels: Derivatives at 0 and the Maclaurin series of $\arcsin$.
All even-order derivatives vanish at $x=0$, not everywhere.
keypoints: $-n^{2}=-n(n-1)-n$; moving this term gives the recurrence.

title: total distance of a bouncing ball
panels: $h=1.5$ m, $r=0.7$: total distance over infinitely many bounces.
Each bounce is a geometric piece.
keypoints: Initial drop once; every completed rebound travels up and down.
$h>0$, $0\le r<1$; the factor $2$ counts the two legs.

title: estimate $\sqrt{51}$ with the binomial series
panels: The safe interior $|u|<1$ permits the binomial expansion; extract $49$.
Both ends of this bound round to $7.1414$.
keypoints: Never feed $x=50$ in: $|x|>1$ diverges.
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ at $n=\frac12$ gives $-\frac18$.

title: partial derivatives of $f=x^{2}y+\sin y$
panels: Freeze the other variable and differentiate normally.
keypoints: Freezing applies only during differentiation.

title: what $L=1$ actually tells you
panels: The signs alternate, so take absolute values first and apply the ratio test.
$L=1$ is inconclusive: the test says nothing, neither convergence nor divergence.
Compare with the harmonic series instead: the absolute series diverges.
keypoints: $L=1$ never means diverge; it means change tools.
Compare with $SUM 1/(1+r)$, a harmonic-type series.

title: exam-style: ball from 3 m with $r=0.6$
panels: (a) total distance, (b) absolute convergence of the series, (c) $D_2$ and a comparison.
Model, sum, test, substitute, check: the standard three-part exam shape.
so the series is absolutely convergent.
Compare the same height: $\frac{D}{h}=4<\frac{17}{3}$ for $r=0.6$ versus $r=0.7$.
At $h=3$ m the totals are $12$ m and $17$ m.
keypoints: Model -> sum -> ratio test -> limit -> numbers -> sanity check.

title: Evaluate $f=x^{2}+xy+y^{2}$ at four points
panels: Both slots are filled at once; $a,b$ are just labels for the same two variables.
Symmetry cannot detect swapped inputs. Check $f(1,2)=1^2+1\cdot2+2^2$ term by term.
keypoints: Both inputs are substituted together.
$f(x,0)=x^{2}$: the $y$-terms die, the function does not.
$f(0,0)=0$ costs no work.

title: First partials of $x^{3}+y^{3}+x^{2}y+xy$
panels: Freeze one variable and differentiate term by term; $x^{2}y$ and $xy$ are products.
$x^{2}y$ contributes $2xy$ to $f_x$ and $x^{2}$ to $f_y$; $xy$ contributes $y$ and $x$.
keypoints: No term is lost in the frozen direction.
$f_y$ still contains $x$: a partial is a function, not a number.
Product terms produce one piece on each side.

title: $f=x^{2}y+x\sin y$: keep the $x$ in front of $\sin$
panels: $x\sin y$ is a product: with respect to $x$ it is $x$ times the constant $\sin y$.
$f(0,y)=0$ for all $y$, so $f_y(0,y)=0$; the formula gives $0+0\cos y=0$.
keypoints: The $x$ before $\sin y$ must survive.
Dropping it gives $f_x=2xy$ and $f_y=x^{2}+\cos y$: the classic error.
$f_y$ keeps $x$ in both terms.

title: Second and mixed partials of $x^{3}+y^{3}+x^{2}y+xy$
panels: Differentiate the first partials again; mixed order must agree when they are continuous.
keypoints: For this smooth polynomial the mixed partials agree.
$\partial_y(2xy+y)=2x+1$; independently $\partial_x(x^2+x)=2x+1$.

title: First and second partials of $e^{x^{2}y}$
panels: Every derivative of the exponential brings down the inner derivative of $x^{2}y$.
keypoints: $4x^{2}y^{2}$ is $(2xy)^{2}$, straight from the product rule.
$f_{yy}=x^{4}E$: $x^{2}$ is brought down twice.
Every answer carries the factor $E$.
At fixed $y$: $E=1+yx^2+O(x^4)$, so $f_{xx}(0,y)=2y$.

title: Relative error of $I=\frac{Ma^2}{2}$
panels: Relative error of $I$ when $M$ gains $0.1\%$ and $a$ loses $0.2\%$.
$I$ is a product of powers, so the relative errors add with their exponents.
For finite changes: $\frac{\Delta I}{I}\approx\frac{\Delta M}{M}+2\frac{\Delta a}{a}$.
keypoints: The exponent $2$ doubles the radius percentage change.
The remaining $uv^2=4\times10^{-9}$ is $4\times10^{-7}$ percentage points.

title: Relative change of $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$
panels: Relative change of $T$ when $l$ gains $2\%$ and $g$ loses $1\%$.
Finite relative changes use $\approx$, not equality.
keypoints: The square root halves the first-order percentages.
A smaller $g$ makes $T$ larger.
Exact change minus linear estimate: about $0.0038438$ percentage points.

title: Change in $z$ from $z^{2}=x^{2}+2y$ at $(3,4)$
panels: $\Delta z$ and $\frac{\Delta z}{z}$ when $x=3$, $y=4$ both rise by $1\%$.
Differentiate the relation implicitly: $z$ is not given explicitly.
Negative branch gives the opposite change.
keypoints: The sign follows the branch $z=\pm\sqrt{17}$; relative changes agree.
Check $z\ne0$ before division; state the branch for a numerical answer.
The differential is a linear estimate, not the exact finite change.

title: Chain rule for $z=e^{xy^{2}}$ with $x=t^{2}$, $y=\sin t$
panels: Both inputs depend on $t$, so both paths contribute.
keypoints: $2xy$ in $z_y$ is where $2t^{2}\sin t\cos t$ comes from.
Substituting first and differentiating in $t$ reproduces the same line.
Two paths, two terms: neither may be dropped.

title: $z=\arctan\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$ with $y=\sin x$
keypoints: $z_x=\frac{1}{1+(\frac{x}{y})^2}\frac{1}{y}=\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}$: include the inner derivative.
The $y$-derivative carries a minus sign.
$\sin x=0$ is excluded: state the domain.

title: Implicit slope from $xy+\sin y=0$
panels: On the curve $z$ is constant, so its total differential vanishes.
keypoints: The denominator $z_y=x+\cos y$ must be nonzero.
The minus sign comes from moving $z_x\,dx$ across.
No solving for $y$ is needed.

title: Heat diffusion: aliasing, three aligned slices, double buffering
panels: A 1-D rod with fixed cold ends, inner points updated by $u_i^{	ext{new}}=u_i+ rac14(u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1})$: find the aliasing bug, write the vectorised version, run 20 steps on 21 points, fix the history snapshots.

The right-hand side must read one old time level, so shared memory between new and old decides correctness before speed; the slices $T[:-2]$, $T[1:-1]$, $T[2:]$ align left, centre and right neighbours.
new = T writes in place: $u_1=0+ rac14(0-0+8)=2$, then $u_2=8+ rac14(2-16+0)=4.5$.
Input and output both end up as $[0,\ 2,\ 4.5,\ 1.125,\ 0]$.
One correct step gives $[0,\ 2,\ 4,\ 2,\ 0]$ and $T$ stays $[0,0,8,0,0]$.
$T^{(k+1)}=	ext{diffuse}(T^{(k)})$ rebinding is safe because the fixed function never writes in place.
The centre spike 100 spreads into a wider, lower, symmetric profile, peak $\approx 12.5$.
history $=[A,B,A,B]$ repeats references; snapshot the initial state and every step with current.copy().
keypoints: One-step check: symmetric, ends stay 0, total heat stays 8.
The time recursion cannot be vectorised away: each step reads the previous one.
Working storage $O(n)$, full history $O(mn)$, total time $O(mn)$.
Copy at both ends: the initial snapshot and every appended step.

title: Differentiate $z=e^{xy^{2}}$ along $x=t^{2}$ and $y=\sin t$
panels: Both inputs move with $t$, so add both dependency paths.
Each partial keeps the exponential and differentiates its exponent.
The two factors of $2$ come separately from differentiating $t^{2}$ and $y^{2}$.
Differentiating its exponent gives $2t(\sin t)^{2}+2t^{2}\sin t\cos t$, matching both paths.
keypoints: Include both paths from $t$ to $z$.
The square belongs to $y$ in $xy^{2}$.
Use radians for trigonometric derivatives.

title: Differentiate $z=\arctan(x/y)$ under $y=\sin x$
panels: Find $\frac{dz}{dx}$ in terms of $x$ for $z=\arctan(x/y)$ and $y=\sin x$.
The original expression requires nonzero $\sin x$.
The constraint moves $y$ with $x$, so include the indirect route.
The $1$ comes from the inverse-tangent derivative; the minus sign comes from differentiating $y^{-1}$.
Substitute $y=\sin x$; no numerical point is specified.
Direct substitution gives $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{\sin x}\right)=\frac{1}{1+(x/\sin x)^{2}}\frac{\sin x-x\cos x}{\sin^{2}x}$.
This simplifies to the same result and retains the original domain restriction.
keypoints: The total derivative includes the moving $y$.
The cosine multiplies only the indirect route.
Simplification does not restore excluded points.

title: Recover $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x$ from $\tan y=x$
panels: For $y=\arctan x$ on the principal branch, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
Undo inverse tangent to obtain $\tan y=x$.
This locally invertible one-variable relation allows reciprocal ordinary derivatives.
The forward derivative is positive, so its reciprocal has no minus sign.
Solving yields the same $\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$, whose denominator is positive for every real $x$.
keypoints: Inverse tangent is not reciprocal tangent.
Undo the inverse function before differentiating.
This reciprocal argument concerns an ordinary one-variable derivative.

title: Find the slope along $xy+\sin y=0$
panels: The output is constant while the inputs remain linked.
A constant output has zero total derivative, avoiding an explicit solution for $y$.
Hold the other input fixed in each partial derivative.
Move $y$ across $0=y+(x+\cos y)\frac{dy}{dx}$ to obtain the minus sign.
The denominator contains $x$ from $xy$ and $\cos y$ from $\sin y$.
No numerical point is given; require a differentiable branch with nonzero $x+\cos y$.
Direct product and chain rules give $y+x\frac{dy}{dx}+\cos y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$.
Collecting the slope terms reproduces the same quotient.
keypoints: A constant output does not freeze both inputs.
Differentiating $xy$ along the curve needs both product-rule terms.
Check the denominator before dividing.

title: Transform the partial derivatives of $z(x,y)$ into polar coordinates
panels: Given $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$, find $\frac{\partial z}{\partial r}$ and $\frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta}$ for differentiable $z(x,y)$.
Each new input changes both old coordinates, so use the two-path chain rule.
Keep the old partials symbolic because $z$ is unspecified.
$\frac{\partial x}{\partial r}=\cos\theta$, $\frac{\partial y}{\partial r}=\sin\theta$ at fixed angle.
$\frac{\partial z}{\partial r}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\cos\theta+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\sin\theta$.
At fixed radius, $\frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta}=-r\sin\theta$ and $\frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta}=r\cos\theta$.
The minus sign comes from cosine; the fixed factor $r$ remains.
Evaluate the old partials at $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$; no numerical $z$ is given.
For $z=x$, the old partials are $1$ and $0$, giving $\frac{\partial z}{\partial r}=\cos\theta$ and $\frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta}=-r\sin\theta$.
Direct differentiation of $z=r\cos\theta$ agrees; at $\theta=0$ the angular derivative is $0$.
keypoints: Radial differentiation holds the angle fixed.
Angular differentiation holds the radius fixed and retains $r$.
An invertible polar coordinate description requires $r>0$.

title: Explain why reversing a polar partial derivative does not give its reciprocal
panels: Compare $\frac{\partial x}{\partial r}$ at fixed $\theta$ with $\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}$ at fixed $y$ for $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$.
Use $r>0$ and nonzero $\cos\theta$ when taking the forward reciprocal.
The held-fixed variables differ, so reconstruct radius from both Cartesian inputs.
At fixed $\theta$, $\frac{\partial x}{\partial r}=\cos\theta$, whose reciprocal is $\frac{1}{\cos\theta}$.
The outer square root gives $\frac{1}{2}$, and differentiating the inner $x^{2}$ gives $2x$.
The numerical factors cancel; fixed $y^{2}$ contributes $0$.
Then $\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}=\frac{1}{2}$, while the reciprocal of $\frac{\partial x}{\partial r}$ is $2$.
The numerical values differ, disproving the general reciprocal claim.
At $\theta=0$ both equal $1$, but special agreement does not establish a general rule.
keypoints: Name the held-fixed variable before reversing a partial.
Use both Cartesian inputs in $r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.
At fixed $y$, the angle generally changes with $x$.

title: Prove the chain-rule identity for $x=s^{2}-t^{2}$ and $y=2st$
panels: For differentiable $u(x,y)$ with $x=s^{2}-t^{2}$ and $y=2st$, prove $s\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}-t\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=2(s^{2}+t^{2})\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}$.
Expand the left side using the known coordinate derivatives.
Keep the old partials symbolic and cancel the $y$ contributions.
$\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}=2s\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+2t\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}$.
$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=-2t\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+2s\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}$.
The factors $2s$, $-2t$, $2t$ and positive $2s$ come from differentiating $s^{2}-t^{2}$ and $2st$.
The outer $-t$ changes the inner $-2t$ into $+2t^{2}$ and the inner $2s$ into $-2st$.
The $y$ coefficient is $2st-2st=0$; the $x$ coefficient is $2s^{2}+2t^{2}$.
Hence $s\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}-t\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=2(s^{2}+t^{2})\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}$.
For $u=x$, the left side is $s(2s)-t(-2t)=2(s^{2}+t^{2})$, matching the right side.
For $u=y$, it is $s(2t)-t(2s)=0$, again matching the right side.
keypoints: Here $u$ is the output and $s,t$ are independent inputs.
The derivative of $2st$ with respect to $t$ is positive $2s$.
Distribute the outer minus to both terms.

title: Prove the chain-rule identity for $x=e^{u}$ and $y=e^{v}$
panels: For differentiable $z(x,y)$ with $x=e^{u}$ and $y=e^{v}$, prove $x\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+y\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}$.
Start from the new-coordinate derivatives on the right and apply the two-path chain rule.
No particular formula for $z$ is needed.
$\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}$.
$\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}$.
$\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}=e^{u}$, $\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}=0$, $\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}=0$, $\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}=e^{v}$.
Absent dependencies give zero; each exponential differentiates to itself.

Substituting gives $\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}=e^{u}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+e^{v}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=x\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+y\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$.
The surviving second partial is with respect to $y$, as supported by the notes.
The transformed function is $e^{u+v}$, so adding its two new partials also gives $2xy$.
keypoints: Zero coordinate factors mean absent dependencies, not a constant output.
The second surviving route keeps $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$.
The exponential transformation gives positive $x$ and $y$.

title: Moment of a force about bar $BC$
panels: The bar is not a coordinate axis, so use axis unit vector, position vector, force in a scalar triple product.
The order is axis direction, position, force.
$\vec M_B=\vec r_{BA}\times\vec F=12\vec i-10\vec j+28\vec k$ kN·m
Negative sign means the vector points from $C$ towards $B$.
keypoints: Unit vector has no metre unit.
Keep the sign when multiplying by $\vec e_{BC}$.

title: Two forces on a crankshaft: sum of moments about $x$
panels: Find the total moment about the $x$ axis.
Only the $x$ component of each cross product is needed.
Superposition adds the two signed contributions.
The two $y$ forces oppose each other, so the sum is smaller than either term.
keypoints: $0.08$ m comes from $80$ mm; the two $z$ offsets have opposite signs.
Do not use $0.16$ and $0.36$ as perpendicular offsets.

title: Reluctance of a car-lifting electromagnet
panels: Find the total reluctance with no air gap.
The core and the roof form one series magnetic path.
Compute each reluctance with its own material, then add.
Shorter but four times less permeable, so the roof must dominate.
keypoints: $1000$ is the turns count, not $\mu_r$.
Reluctance adds for a series path.

title: Minimum holding current for a $2000$ kg car
panels: Hold $2000$ kg with two pole faces of $4\times10^{-4}$ m$^{2}$ each.
At the threshold, magnetic force balances weight.
Use both faces for force, one section for flux.
$7.85$ T is far above steel saturation, so this is a linear idealisation only.
keypoints: Two faces give force; one section carries flux.
$9.81$ m/s$^{2}$ is the $g$ used here.

title: Rod and tube sharing one load
panels: Tube and coaxial rod, equal length $L$, same rigid end plates.
Two unknown member forces, so equilibrium alone is not enough.
Add equal-extension compatibility and the elastic law.
$EA$ has units N, so $FL/(EA)$ has units m.
keypoints: Equal strain does not mean equal stress.
$EA$ terms add because the members act in parallel.

title: Cylinder with four tie rods: shared axial load
panels: $P=20$ MPa, $R=40$ mm, $t=4$ mm, four rods $d=8$ mm.
Wall and rods share the end load: one equilibrium equation.
Equal axial extension gives the second equation.
keypoints: $5.25=336/64$ is the area ratio.
$\sigma_r\approx-20$ MPa is about one tenth of the hoop stress.

title: Work done by a constant force along a slope
panels: $\vec r_1=(35\vec i+51\vec j)$ m, $\vec r_2=(100\vec i+71\vec j)$ m.
Constant force $\vec F=(43\vec i+50\vec j)$ N.
Constant force and known endpoints, so work is the dot product of force with displacement.
Force magnitude alone is not enough; direction matters.
All components positive, so positive work is expected.
Each product is N·m, which is a joule.
keypoints: Subtract end minus start, not the reverse.
Work is J; moment is N·m; different quantities.

title: A block resting on a slope
panels: Stationary block of weight $W$ on a slope of angle $\alpha$.
Find the normal force $N$ and friction $f$.
The block is at rest, so balance forces along and perpendicular to the plane.
Do not assume friction is already at its maximum.
At $\alpha=0$: $f=0$ and $N=W$, which matches a flat floor.
keypoints: Normal force is perpendicular to the slope, not vertical.
Friction opposes the tendency to slip.

title: Estimating $\mu_s$ from the tilt angle
panels: The block starts to slip at about $20$ degrees.
Estimate the coefficient of static friction.
At impending slip the friction is at its maximum, so $f=\mu_sN$.
$\tan0=0$ and $\tan$ increases here, so a positive value below $1$ is sensible.
keypoints: Set the calculator to degrees.
The angle was approximate, so this is an estimate.

title: Induced emf: sign and magnitude
panels: A coil of $N$ turns sits in a changing flux $\phi(t)$.
State the induced emf and its direction rule.
Faraday gives the magnitude; Lenz fixes the direction.
Use a consistent positive direction for flux and emf.
The induced current opposes the change in flux.
It does not oppose every field or every motion.
$\phi$ in Wb, $t$ in s, so $e$ comes out in V.
Steady flux means $d\phi/dt=0$, so no emf is induced.
keypoints: Open circuit: emf exists but no sustained current.
More turns or faster change gives a bigger emf.

title: Why a brushed DC machine needs a commutator
panels: A single winding turns between fixed poles.
Explain why the current must be reversed twice per turn.
The conductor forces reverse when the winding passes the neutral position.
Without switching, the torque would reverse too.
$F=Bli$ on both sides, in opposite directions.
The forces act along the axle line, so the moment about the axis falls to zero.
The segments swap brushes every half turn, so the coil current reverses.
The torque keeps one sign, but still pulsates with position.
keypoints: Brushes stay fixed; segments rotate.
One-way torque does not mean constant torque.

title: polar partials: $\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}$ is not the reciprocal
panels: Show it equals $\cos\theta$, the direct answer.
keypoints: A partial derivative freezes the other independent variables, and which ones are independent is a choice.
$1/\cos\theta$ alone is a partial derivative of $x/\cos\theta$, just not the one asked for.
$\arctan(y/x)$ is quadrant-dependent, but its partials are not.

title: $f=x^{2}y$ about $(1,2)$: second-order expansion
panels: Expand $f(x,y)=x^{2}y$ about $(1,2)$ to second order, with $h=x-1$, $k=y-2$.
School algebra expands this function exactly,
so the truncation can be checked.
keypoints: The $\frac{1}{2}$ acts on all three second-order terms, including $2hk f_{xy}$.
The dropped term is cubic in $h$ only, because there is no $y^{2}$ term.
At $h\approx0.1$ the error is already in the third decimal.

title: completing the square: the sign test for $\Delta f$
panels: Rewrite $\Delta f=\frac{1}{2}(ah^{2}+2bhk+ck^{2})$ so its sign can be read.
so a sum of squares isolates the sign.
keypoints: Completing the square is an identity, not an approximation.
$ac-b^{2}$ is the correction term the square leaves behind.
The test silently assumes $a\neq0$ and says nothing when $ac-b^{2}=0$.

title: four stationary points: two saddles, one max, one min
panels: Find all stationary points and classify each.
so look for a combination killing the mixed term.
keypoints: Two quadratics normally give four solutions; two means one was lost.
$b=0$ exactly on the line $y=x$, which checks the algebra.
Signed square roots make the table the easiest place to slip.

title: when $a=0$: $f=x^{3}+y^{2}$ is a saddle
panels: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x,y)=x^{3}+y^{2}$.
The test divides by $a$, so watch that step.
A formula that divides must be checked
at the value where the divisor vanishes.
keypoints: With $a=0$ the quadratic test carries no information.
The truncation dropped the whole $h$ direction.
Saddles do not always look like saddles.

title: constant-pressure expansion: where enthalpy comes from
panels: Gas trapped under a weighted piston, heat $Q_{12}$ added slowly.
Weight fixed, atmosphere fixed, so mechanical equilibrium gives $p_{1}=p_{2}$.
Constant $p$ lets it leave the integral.
keypoints: $U$, $p$, $V$ are all properties, so $U+pV$ is a property.
$Q=\Delta H$ is a constant-pressure special case, not a general law.
Sign convention here is $Q-W=\Delta U$.

title: why $c_{p}-c_{v}=R$
panels: The state equation already tells us $pv$.
No path is chosen, so the result holds for every state.
$R$ is constant so it survives as itself.
keypoints: Do not treat $v$ as constant while differentiating: use the state relation.
The $R$ here is the same specific gas constant as in $pv=RT$.
$c_{p}>c_{v}$ because constant pressure also pays for work.

title: one isentrope, three forms
panels: All three describe the same process,
so eliminating one variable must reproduce the others.
keypoints: The three constants are different numbers; do not carry one across forms.
All three need adiabatic, reversible, ideal gas.
The isentrope is steeper than the isotherm through the same point.

title: rigid tank: why $c_{v}$ is the right specific heat
panels: Rigid tank, heat $Q_{12}$ added to reach state 2.
The work term can be removed by physical argument,
keypoints: Rigidity only removes boundary work; check shafts and diaphragms.
$m$ appears only when converting total to specific.
Heat here is not an enthalpy change, so $c_{v}$ not $c_{p}$.
